utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I understand you have a matter or some matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I do have two matters that I want to deal with. The first is something that pertains to witness T-19. We sought protective measures for him, and pursuant to your decision those measures were approved. Now that the witness is about to appear in court he would like to give evidence without any protective measures. So first the thing I would like you to do before he comes in the courtroom, I would like to ask you whether you are prepared to approve this change; and the second matter pertains to the evidence of other witnesses to be heard. Witness T-60 is already in The Hague. He is due to be examined tomorrow. He arrived last night and I will be proofing him for his testimony, but the last two witnesses T-57 and T-25, will be arriving tomorrow evening around 9.00 p.m.. You know that there is a rule in place to protect the witnesses. The witnesses cannot be proofed immediately upon their arrival, but, if necessary, I can do the proofing by midnight with those two witnesses. But I would like to ask you, if possible, to hold the -- our session on Thursday, the 26th in the afternoon. I believe that it would be possible because not many trials are going on. That would enable me to proof my witnesses properly. So these were two issues that I wanted to raise and to ask your assistance on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well,, as for the first, trials are ordinarily public, so we naturally would have no difficulty with that. For the second, I will have to consult. But is there any difficulty with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution doesn't have a problem, but, of course, Mr. Tapuskovic, this comes very late, and many persons would have made arrangements for travel. But I have to ask you, how long do you think this witness will be? The two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two witnesses, yes, I have two witnesses ready for today, and that should take us through the whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm talking about Thursday afternoon. Thursday afternoon when you're asking that we sit -- instead of sitting in the morning. I'm trying to see whether we can accommodate you. So, in that regard, I'm asking how long will the witnesses take?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the circumstances, I will try to take even less time that you have allotted to me so that we can complete their evidence so that they don't have to come back. I have a total of two and a half hours, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For both witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just looking at the time statement that was circulated and if I'm not mistaken, we're talking about the two witnesses for Thursday who would be T-25 and T-60. For T-25, there's an hour and a quarter allotted for each party, and for T-60 an hour and a half allotted for each party presently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Your Honours. My learned colleague does not have all the information at her disposal. Because Witness T-60 will be examined tomorrow and I have just one witness for tomorrow, because the other two will be arriving later with -- due to some extraordinary efforts put in by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, they will be able to arrive tomorrow night. So, for Thursday I have witnesses T-57 and T-25 lined up. I think one of them is due to testify for half an hour and the another one for a bit longer. I think that we already have this information, and I don't think that we will have any problems finishing their evidence so that they don't have to appear before this Trial Chamber again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I stand corrected. That's correct. T-57 is allotted half an hour for each party and T-25 an hour and a quarter for each party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that makes three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At best, just under one full court day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe we will have to stop at 6.00. So we'll have to try to conclude the testimony of both witnesses by 6.00 p.m. Could we start earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Prosecution certainly available to start earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we start earlier? What are the logistics involved in starting earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand there is a courtroom available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I need 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The problem is that my colleague here, Judge Harhoff, is -- he's in a case in the morning, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... For 15 minutes. But I need 15 minutes between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. With a tremendous effort and worthy effort on the part of Judge Harhoff, he has agreed that we can start at 2.00 p.m. So he will have a 15-minute break after the end of his first trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will endeavour to complete my examination in even less time than allotted to me with the exception, of course, of this witness who is due to give evidence for only half an hour, that's T-57, half an hour. That's really the time that I have to use as efficiently as is possible, and I will also try to use all my time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will start at 2.00 p.m. on Thursday and finish at 6.00. Then let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you first have to state your full name to the Chamber, to the Judges, to the Prosecution. And I would therefore like to devote the first few questions to your background, your personal details. Could you please tell the Judges your full name?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Vlastimir Glavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 20th of March, 1964?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Hadzici, in the municipality of Sarajevo, in Donja Bioca?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Donja Bioca, municipality of Hadzici. That's one of the municipalities in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to wait for me to complete my question fully and please observe the cursor on your screen. When it stops, then you can start your answer. You completed your elementary education in Tarcin, Hadzici and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from the high school in Hadzici in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the conflict broke out, you were a haulier, you had your own private business?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you lived in your family home in Hadzici, in Donja Bioca?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to warn you once again. Please don't answer before you see that the cursor has stopped, otherwise we're going to have problems. I explained this to you yesterday during our proofing session. Witness, could you please explain to the Judges what units were you in at one point and when?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It was in late 1993. I was at Ilidza, in the Ilidza police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many police officers were there in this police station?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: There were 21 police officers in the station where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you must not start answering immediately when I complete my question. You have to wait for five or six seconds before you start your answer. You have to pay attention to this cursor, otherwise the interpreters are going to be in trouble, the Defence is going to be in trouble and so will the Chamber. You said 21?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what area is that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Ilidza. Ilidza that was the reserve police station at Ilidza, my station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're going too fast again. Please focus on the screen in front of you and don't start your answer before the cursor has stopped. So did you know at all anything about the police units that were there in various police units in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, about four to 500 people in the area of the entire CSB Sarajevo, the Security Services centre Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what kinds of duties did you have as a police officer when you joined them in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: After I was released from the Silos camp, I was in a very bad shape. And after I recuperated a couple of months later, I joined this station, where I mostly worked in the duty room, because I was not fit to go to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges how long did you spend in the camp and why were you in such a bad shape at the time when you joined the unit?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would submit that his time in detention in the Silos camp and treatment there is irrelevant to this trial against General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you explain how it is relevant, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be dealing with his stay in the Silos camp later. He spent time there, and that pertains to the very outbreak of the conflict, the reasons why he was arrested. The circumstances in which the conflict broke out. I want to bring him to this time. I knew that the Prosecution would be objecting. I wanted first to bring him to the time-period relevant for the indictment. But the Chamber always allowed me to deal with what was happening at the outbreak of the conflict with other witnesses. This is very important for this case, highly relevant, because it speaks to the suffering that those people went through in those camps. If the Chamber deems that to be irrelevant, then, I don't think that I should have dealt with any other issues that pertain to the outbreak of the conflict. If it is not irrelevant for -- to determine why this man was placed under arrest, when he joined the forces to defend his home and then was put in a camp for that reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would think you can deal with the circumstances leading to his detention, but his actual detention and what happened to him in detention I would think is not particularly significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be guided by what you just said, but my next few questions will perhaps clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please describe to us what condition were you in, why were you unable to join in any action at this time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: After seven months of detention in the Silos camp I weighed 40 kilos, and I had had 75 kilos at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you do at first in this police station?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I was a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when were you able -- but first, tell me, this police force, the 21 police officers, what did they do in the police station and in the Ilidza area?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: We did police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who was in charge, who was the head?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Dragisa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters did not catch the last name of the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you start joining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreter didn't hear the last name of the superior. You said your immediate superior was Dragisa. What's the last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragisa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there another name? Is that the only name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kapetina. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember when Dragomir Milosevic became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was sometime in early August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in what combat actions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did you participate first?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That was on the Nisici plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: In late 1994, October/November, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And your police unit that had 21 officers, under whose command was it on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: We were part of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us how many such events were there in October/November and all the way to the end of the year that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Three, four, five clashes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in those clashes that you took part in, were there any casualties, civilian or among the soldiers, in this area?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. A colleague of mine, Nenad Kuvac was killed. And later on, when he was buried he had been chained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite clear. I didn't understand what you mean and the Chamber cannot understand what you mean. Was he chained at the position or what?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: He was wounded and he was dragged away. And after a month, he was exchanged, and then it was ascertained that his legs had been chained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are mentioning the death of your colleague. But were there any other victims among the soldiers or civilians at the time in Hadzici, Nisici, Ilidza where you participated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So far, Your Honour, the witness has actually only said he took part in actions at the Nisici plateau and he hasn't cited any other locations. So perhaps the question could be rephrased so that the answers could be properly founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the conflicts and clashes at Nisici, since you were present in Ilidza, were there any clashes in that period of time around Hadzici and in Ilidza in particular, where you were a part of the -- of a police station?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. But I said at the start that I was assigned to the front lines more rarely than others due to the condition I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely why I'm putting this question to you. Since you spent more time in Ilidza and went to Nisici only rarely due to your health condition, my question for you was whether in the fighting at Nisici, Ilidza, and Hadzici there were any victims among soldiers, in civilians, specifically in -- in the areas that were quite densely populated.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. At Ilidza and Hadzici, as these were areas that were under daily shelling, there were quite a few victims among civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, before we proceed to talk about the fighting, in the time-period we have just referred to and in the subsequent period, when did you take up arms for the first time and what were the circumstances surrounding this event?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I took up arms for the first time before these clashes broke out. The conflict in Hadzici began on the 10th and the 11th of May. I lived in a village 12 kilometres away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it we're talking about 1992 now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What time is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're speaking of the early days of the conflict, of 1992. Unless we deal with these matters none of the subsequent events can be understandable. I am in a situation where I cannot at all begin to work as a Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand -- I didn't understand Ms. Edgerton to be objecting on that basis. She simply wanted to know the time, the year. It's 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go on explaining what you've just started to explain before you were interrupted. What were the circumstances in which you first took up arms. You mentioned a date, I believe, and it was quite evident which year you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I said that the conflict in Hadzici started already on the 10th or 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which -- of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, what prompted you to take up arms. What happened?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Buses were passing through my village every day, holding members of the Muslim army. They attacked the part of Hadzici held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what the situation was in your village. Can you be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seem to be on my feet constantly on matters of relevance but I'm rising again on the relevance of this portion of the testimony. We had begun in 1994 leading into 1995 the period of the indictment, but with respect, Your Honours, I would submit the reason why somebody takes up arms in 1992 is irrelevant to the case against General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been the situation so far. When I started dealing with 1992, the Prosecution and in particular my learned friend here from the Prosecution, would stand up and object that this was not covered by the -- the case against Mr. Milosevic or, that rather that I should also deal with the roots of it. Now that I'm trying to deal with the roots of the conflict which led to the events involving Mr. Milosevic, I'm being prevented from doing that as well. I believe that I'm led to explain each and every time what the relevance of my questions is all the time and I have been doing this. I believe that the goal behind such an attitude of my learned friends is simply to obstruct what I'm trying to get from the witness. Is it not relevant to know what was going on in 1992, why he was arrested and how he was treated as a prisoner? Then if it is not really relevant then I have no place being here. I would be more than happy to have started dealing with the 10th of August, 1994, rather than with anything else. But I'm constantly being asked here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you may continue with the examination, but I must say that I find it strange that you would spend so much time on contextual historical matters. In my view, the case is not going to be determined on what happened in 1992. Move on to the period that is relevant, most relevant to the indictment. So continue, but I don't believe that your client is going to benefit from dwelling on these contextual and historical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not dealing with the background of the case. I'm dealing with the fate this man has suffered. Let me tell you something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to deal with matters that are relevant to this person without touching on any historical matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours. You can even censure me in this, but have I the duty to pursue my Defence case in the way I deem relevant and of course it will be up to you to decide whether these matters were relevant or not. I believe that the fate that has -- this man has suffered is quite relevant. If you believe that it is out of place for me to do that, I am in your hands. If you believe that I'm dealing with the historical background rather than with any relevant matters, then I am in your hands to decide what I should do next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I told you to carry on. Why don't you carry on and stop arguing. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you were engaging in the fighting on those rare occasions when your health condition permitted you to, what kept you going in all these actions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: What kept me going was the fear, the suffering and the hardship that I experienced in the Silos camp. I wanted to make sure that I never ended up in their hands again, in the hands of those that tortured me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At those moments, did you harbour any specific intentions with regard to the civilians on the other side? This is as far as I can go in putting this question to you.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I never, ever did anything to harm anyone. I wouldn't do so now. I felt pity for the civilians of Muslim, Serb and Croat ethnicities of all of them, regardless of their religious beliefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the circumstances leading to your arrest were?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I was arrested because I wielded a rifle, and I had a rifle simply to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long were you in captivity?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which camp was that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: The Silos camp at Tarcin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I have already ruled earlier that I did not want to hear that. Move on to something else. You have led evidence as to the circumstances leading to his arrest and he was in detention. Then move on to -- move on to the next area of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next topic could be whether the prisoners were used as human shields with a view to protecting the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in their actions. Were prisoners used as human shields in the actions mounted by the BH army, if you will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually, Mr. Tapuskovic directed the question to Your Honours, as to whether or not you would allow it. I'm on my feet over the same objection, absolutely the same objection, Your Honour; it's irrelevant. These things are all right for contextual matters that might help us all better assess the background to the indictment against the accused. But this isn't a trial, with respect, Your Honours, about who started the war, why someone decided to fight or what abuses might have been perpetrated in detention facilities not under the control of the man who is presently on trial, Your Honour, and outside of the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber is not allowing the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me think about this, whether I have any questions left at all. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you spoke of the clashes and fighting in 1994. What were the subsequent developments like? What was the situation like in late 1994 and in early 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: As I said, in late 1994 there was fighting going on which was followed by a truce. The truce lasted until early May or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Next came an offensive by the Muslim forces against the territories held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was it like and how long did it last, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It lasted from early May until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I have to go through this more quickly and deal with matters of relevance, what happened on the 28th of August, 1995, in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1995, I got married. It was the day of my wedding at Vrelo Bosne, Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What time was the wedding to take place and what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, among Orthodox Serbs the Feast of the Assumption is a major feast. There was a mass. And my wedding was scheduled to take place at around 12.00, ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: As the wedding ceremony drew to a close, as the wedding guests started leaving the church, shells started falling from the direction of Igman all around the church and my wedding guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many shells fell?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Three shells fell in the immediate vicinity of the church, and a total of about 12 -- 12 shells fell in the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many wedding guests were injured and was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: 47 people were wounded, and one person was killed. That was my wife's cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, DD00-3178, and I would like you to answer some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is obviously probably the most difficult time of this witness's life and if is going to be prolonged by going through questions about this document which is an investigative report on the incident prepared by the RS CSB, the RS police forces, I'm quite happy that Mr. Tapuskovic tender the document. I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you want to tender the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honours, no, not before the witness is able to confirm some things in this document, and not before I have dealt with some issues in this document, because I don't want to just gloss over those things. This is why this witness wanted to talk about this, why he decided to do so without protective measures. I may not be tendering this document, but I think that my learned colleague cannot really manage the way I present my case. Because if we can't hear this, this is the 28th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: She's just trying to be helpful --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you must know that Ms. Edgerton was only trying to be helpful because the witness is obviously in some pain and grief over this and he's upset, so she was trying to spare him more of that upset. That's all she was trying to do, it seems to me. Not to manage your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness had been upset enough during his nine months stay in the camp, you did allow him to describe this. But He wants to describe this because is this the 28th of August, and despite Judge Harhoff's wishes, I will be presenting this. I have already cut down my examination. You are in charge of it, but so if you believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Get along with it. Get along with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, there is nothing here but -- let me not go into anything here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have not raised my voice at all. I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, could you please look at this document. Look at the date and the heading. The date and what it says in the subject line -- no. To cut this short, what is the -- the title of this document? What you see here, official report, do you see that? Can you tell us what is it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: The ministry --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: The official report in the afternoon hours of the 28th of August, 1995, the criminal investigation service of this CSB was informed that between 12.30 and 1300 hours on the same day, a number of mortar shells were fired from the positions of the so-called army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the Serbian Orthodox church devoted to Saint Sava in the Vrelo Bosne settlement, in front of which there were at the time a mass of believers and a wedding party, as well as at the neighbouring settlements, Vrelo Bosne and Plandiste in the Ilidza municipality and that a number of persons were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: May I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now could we please look at page 2 in the English version and page 2 in the B/C/S version, the second paragraph, if you could just read the first couple of sentences there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has some problems, some needs, and perhaps it would be a good idea -- did I understand you correctly? The witness must leave the courtroom for a couple of minutes because he has bladder problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take a short adjournment. Five minutes. --- Break taken at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, so we're on page 2 now, second paragraph. Could you please just read this. Read aloud.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: "The explosion of these shells" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I said the second paragraph. That starts with the words "the explosion." Is this where you started?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please start there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: "The explosion of these shells killed Jadranka Vitor, born in 1961, mother of two underage children, residing in Hadzici, while 46 persons were seriously or slightly wounded in the church yard and six persons in the Vrelo Bosne and Plandiste settlements. At the same time, the facade of the western wall of the church was damaged by shrapnel in about 30 places."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You looked at the photographs that were appended to this file and do these photographs, because I don't want to exhibit them, correspond with the site and the scenes that could be observed there after this incident?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that ten or 12 shells fell?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of your relatives, your closest relatives, wounded?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. In this shelling, my father was wounded and so were my two brothers, my cousin, and a little girl who was also my cousin. She was one and a half years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to tender this whole document into evidence. It's been translated into English and there are photographs that are attached to it. There's no need for me to show those photographs in courtroom. They contain the -- among them is a photograph of the dead body of this woman and I would like now to like to tender this document DD00-3178, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The -- I would have no objection, as I had indicated previously, to the translated text of the document which is seven pages without any photographs because I have not seen the photographs being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what you are saying, then, is you -- you object to the photographs being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've simply not seen them and, in any case, if they are photographs of what is described in a detailed version in this official -- in a detailed way in this official report, they're simply redundant. So I'm happy if the seven-page report is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few more questions. I would like to try and finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was at 12.30 and 1.00, according to this record. What did you do afterwards, you and all the others?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: After the shelling, we drove the wounded people to the Zica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me, first of all, were you yourself injured?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I and my wife were not wounded. We were the only members of the close family who were not wounded. All the rest were wounded and my brother was hospitalised for ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn anything from the media during the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I heard -- I heard it in the media that there had been a massacre at Markale, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, this was at 12.30, around 1.00, 12.30, 1.00, do you remember what was it said in the reports? At what time did this incident at Markale take place?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was at 11.00 or ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know anything about air bombs?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I only know about that when NATO air-strikes -- when NATO carried out air-strikes against Serbian positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when was that in relation to the 20th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It was two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And since I have some more time, I would like to ask you to tell me, Ilidza and this place where you were, what was it -- its geographic position in relation to its environs?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Ilidza and Hadzici are surrounded, were surrounded on all sides by the Muslim forces because they held the highest ground, the BH army held the highest ground. And shellings were a daily occurrence in Hadzici and Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you not to hit the desk because it can be heard. What did the civilians do in order to protect themselves against the BH army fire?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Some concrete walls were put up, I don't know how to describe it, in order to protect the population against shells and snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show you one photograph and ask you whether it has anything to do with Ilidza. That's DD00-4233.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the direction of Stup.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who held the positions at Stup, and I mean the military positions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: The forces of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document into evidence as a Defence exhibit. And this was my final question in relation to this document. Can we please have DD00-4233 admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D344, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton is there any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One moment to double-check, please, Your Honours, if you could indulge me with my colleague Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would hope only about ten minutes worth of questions, Your Honours, no longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go back to that unfortunate incident we spoke about with the shelling, with regard to the shelling which followed your wedding ceremony. And I note that in your testimony you read out something from a document that's been exhibited saying that, in fact I'll read exactly to what you wrote: The official report in the afternoon hours of 28 August, the criminal investigation service of the CSB was informed that between half past 12.00 and 1.00 on that day, a number of mortar shells were fired from the positions of the so-called army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at -- in fact, the area where your ceremony had taken place. Do you remember reading that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Just now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So how, sir, do you know that fire had come from territory held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I know because the forces of the BH army were up at Igman. They held Igman and that was where the shells came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- and you've said in your testimony that Hadzici and Ilijas -- sorry, Ilidza were in fact surrounded as you described it, by forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, in fact, what you're saying is since you were surrounded, it's logical to assume that when a shell lands in your area, it comes from the people who are surrounding you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like just then to move on one final area, and it's with respect to the photograph that you spoke about before which showed passive anti-sniping barricades in an area with which you were familiar. And I would just like to know whether you have any knowledge at all of similar barricades being erected in areas of Bosnian-held territory nearby.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what do I know about it. Yes, there were some down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's because you had seen them, had some glimpses of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I would just like to show you a couple of pictures of these sort of barricades that come from the area of Bosnian-held Dobrinja and ask, based on your recollection, if it's consistent with what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those would have ter number 03473, please. Might need to turn the picture -- there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that generally consistent with the type of things that you might have seen on - if I can call it that way - the other side, as well as on your side?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know where this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's in Bosnian-held Dobrinja, sir, and it was taken in very early 1996. And my only question is: Is this generally consistent with what you might have seen and perhaps -- there's a couple of photographs here. Perhaps we could move to the next page in this list, in this series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if this was slip of the tongue, because it says here that it was taken in 1996. What has it got to do with anything? It says here that it was in Dobrinja. That was Bosnian-held territory, if I understand English correctly, and then it says 1996. Was it in -- taken in 1996 and, if so, what does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'd like to ask the same question too. Is it in 1996 and what is the relevance of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The pictures were taken in early February 1996, Your Honours, immediately prior to the reintegration and as the witness had said, he was aware of similar passive anti-sniping barriers being erected in Bosnian-held territory and he had seen some from time to time. I'm simply asking if this is consistent with what -- with his recollection, with what he had seen at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't consider it relevant, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine, thank you, Your Honours. If you could remove the picture from the screen. I don't have any other questions then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I presume you have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have just several questions. I don't know if we have time. I only need a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On what? I mean, there was hardly any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely because of the questions my learned friend put to the witness about what he was able to see from Ilidza in the direction of any -- in any direction concerning Muslim-held territory. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, were you able to see anything from Ilidza as concerns the Bosnian-held part of Sarajevo, were you able to see any of these territories?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Not from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honours, that has nothing to do with the two questions that I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think -- unless you have other questions we are stopping. Do you have other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have other questions. But my learned friend from the Prosecution asked the witness whether he was able to see such scenes in Bosnian-held territory as was shown in the photograph. No part of Bosnian-held territory could be seen from Ilidza because of the Stup hill, Sokolje, Mojmilo and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Witness, that concludes your testimony. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. And you may leave now with us as we take the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the witness is going to make his declaration. Let the witness make his declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the other witness's microphone be switched on, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please switch on the second microphone. And Mr. Tapuskovic, you may begin. But, Mr. Waespi, did you have a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, a procedural issue, but we can deal with it at the end of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin then, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness T-4. I have to introduce myself. You know that I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. We have already discussed the matters we will deal with today. Can I remind you that you have to wait for my question to be entered into the transcript, which you see in front of you on this screen before you start answering. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please state your name to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Slobodan Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 18th of March, 1952?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your primary school, your secondary graphic design school, in Sarajevo, as well as the administration college?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the start of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Sarajevo, you worked for the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as head of graphic design?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, how long you worked for the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I worked there until the end of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And why did you stop working there at the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: As I came to work on the 28th of April of 1992, in the government building, I came across armed men there, men I didn't know. I went past them, and got into my office. I was called by a colleague of mine who told me with the very best of intentions that I ought to leave the premises as I had no business being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that date, did you experience anything in the flat you had in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. I had a flat at what is today Kolovarska Street -- Darovalaca Krvi Street. Men came to my flat allegedly searching for weapons. They accused me of being a sharpshooter, of wielding a sniper. I had never owned any weapons and I thought I'd be safe if I went to the government building and joined the colleagues I worked with there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to make matters you're testifying about clear, I have to use a map of Sarajevo briefly, which is document 65 ter, document 2872. Could you show us where the government building was and where your flat was? I should also like you to indicate those places with circles and you will also place some letters next to that in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be zoomed in a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please indicate where the government building was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it with the letter "V". Please circle the place where your flat was and mark it with the letter "K".

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After the events of April, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I went to Miljevici, where my parents were. I was -- I really felt bad about everything that had happened. And then afterwards, I went to the government building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, please, wait. Now that you have indicated this, can you indicate the location of Miljevici on this map. Where your family flat is. It's somewhere in the south, I believe, and you seem to be looking at the top of the map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it with the letter "M".

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say you went there to your parents' home?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please take it slowly. You came to your parents' home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever return to the flat you had in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On your arrival at your parents' home, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: In the morning, I went to the government building where I was charged with preparing and editing the official bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please. You said the government building. Did you go back to the government of the -- did you go back to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- wait, please, till I put the question. I'm really surprised at hearing your answers in view of your profession. When you said the government, which government did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, you hastily answered before my question was entered into the transcript. Please wait for my question to be entered in the transcript fully before you answer. What did you do then in the government of Republika Srpska and where was the building located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The government of Republika Srpska was located at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties in the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait. You're a journalist. How come you're finding it difficult to deal with such a situation. You're faced with it everyday. Please take it slowly. Can I have your answer now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I was editing the official bulletin, the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, where laws and by-laws of Republika Srpska were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which route would you take to reach Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I had to take the Miljevici-Lukavica-Tilava route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. Why are you mentioning Lukavica in this context? Did Lukavica have anything to do with the duties you had to perform?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I had to take that route in order to reach Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw this route on the map, and I will have a question for you. Please find Lukavica first. Is that really difficult?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It's not shown on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please approximate the route?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I can't draw the route, because there is no Lukavica, Tilava or Trebevic. I really can't do that on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps the map can be saved and then scrolled down where I would imagine the route can be -- can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can that be done? Yes. Well, let's do that then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. There was a suggestion that the map be scrolled down and then save it. Save it. Yes, you can save it, yes. But we're not admitting it yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's possible. I think we have to save it in the format in which it is now but I'm sure the court officers will be able to explain that better than I can. But now we have no markings at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm told it has been saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw the route on the map; namely, the route you took in doing your job, which we will discuss from Miljevici across Lukavica to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to be zoomed in a bit further and scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now I believe you can do that, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I have Miljevici and Lukavica. I don't have Tilava, oh no, I have Tilava as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What have you drawn there? This isn't something that I asked from you. What is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This is the route I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how would you reach Pale from all these locations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I took a detour to Tvrdinici, Zvorovi [phoen], beneath Jahorina down to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw an arrow indicating where all that is in relation to the locations you have marked.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you would next go to Pale. Can you mark the arrow with the letter "P"? What do the circles represent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The places. The place from which I set out, the place I passed through and then the place I reached before I moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you couldn't go directly from Miljevici to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now explain this, why were you not able to go there directly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: We weren't able to go across Trebevic because the forces of the BH army from the observation post, from Zvesdra, I will tell you now what it is called, they fired on the road. They kept it under their control and we couldn't take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Trebevic. Can you tell us more specifically which section of the road that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wait for the question to finish. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Zlatiste, Ravne, Brus, and that would take us to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was going on on the road or, rather on the section of the road passing through Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Zlatiste and Andza's house as it was called, were held by the BH army with heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Zlatiste and Andza's house were under the control of the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please give it a thought. The road across Zlatiste, in whose hands was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The road across Zlatiste was held by the BH army. It controlled the road from Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the very road, who controlled the road itself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The road was held by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the road was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what do you precisely mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: What I meant was that from Colina Kapa, there was constant fire on the road making it impossible for anyone to move along the road on foot, let alone in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I must caution you that you -- sometimes you come fairly close to cross-examining your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness actually failed to understand some of the questions I asked, and perhaps this caused me to get close to the cross-examination style. But he, in fact, did not understand what I wanted to get from him, and I asked for some clarifications. I wasn't leading him in any way. I will try to avoid that at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In all those years, did you ever pass through Zlatiste at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could those two maps be saved in this form as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a clarification as to the period. I understand that the witness is speaking about the period 1992 to 1995 when he answers the question, all those years. So, is the evidence that during the conflict he never took that road? I'm not sure of the time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as for the latter I think can you ask that in cross-examination. But will you just clarify the time-period that you're speaking of, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the time-period between 1992 and 1995. But at times it was possible to pass through during cease-fire periods, and that was sometime between August 1994 and January 1995, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could both maps be saved as a Defence exhibit then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibits D345 and D346, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you tell the Judges how long you remained working in the Republika Srpska government, working on the publication of the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Until the 13th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I founded Sarajevske Srpske Novine, the Sarajevo Serbian paper at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you get to work in those days, what route did you take?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I went from Miljevici via Vraca to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Every day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't answer immediately. And what was your experience in 1993, 1994, 1995, as you took this road?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: On this map where I drew in the Miljevici-Lukavica route in the area of the memorial park at Vraca, it was very difficult to pass through there in the vicinity of Debelo Brdo because of the shelling and gun-fire from Debelo Brdo. I failed to mention that when I talked about the route that I took to Lukavica. That route also passes through Vraca, and it goes down to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from the memorial park which was under threat, as you just described to us and then onwards to Grbavica, how did you move? Was it safe to move there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No. It was not safe, because the road dips down and it goes towards Sarajevo. It's the Debisa Nujica Street, I think it was called. There were some blankets put up, some curtains so that people would be out of sight as they moved down towards Grbavica and then warnings were posted about sites that were targeted by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, did you have to -- or, rather, how often did you go to Grbavica because of your job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I went down to Grbavica and came back every day five or six times. Because of my job, I had to bring the materials to -- to the desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time have weapons as you went to work and came back home or when you moved anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No. I was never armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what did you actually do in this newspaper that was called Sarajevske Srpkse Novine?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I edited the newspaper. In order to inform the population about the developments at the front, the confrontation lines, what was happening at Grbavica, Vojkovici, Lukavica, in those areas, Pale and so on, the quantities of humanitarian aid that had come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in charge of the distribution of this information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us who did that this information reached, this information that you had, and that you then disseminated, who did it reach?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The information could reach the citizens and the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which citizens, which troops?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The citizens of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to disseminate this information to some other recipients?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. We often wanted to disseminate this information, those reports to various media outlets that -- whose crews would come to Grbavica. But the newspapers and the reports in them did not reach as far as Belgrade let alone any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were you visited by people from major media houses in the world and what would happen when they came, in the sense that I've been asking you about, and what you have been answering?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. CNN came. Most of the major houses would come and we would give them our information, show them the photographs, but it was never made public. They never ran any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was -- what stories did they run that you as the editor of this newspaper, as you as the editor were able to notice? What did those large media houses publish always?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I personally believe that the media that came to the area of -- controlled by the Republika Srpska army and the BH army, that they had applied different standards. From the areas controlled by the BH army, all the reports were published, and very little was published of what was going on in the Republika Srpska army controlled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an event in March 1995, in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go slow. Nothing will get recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, two girls were killed in front of the shopping building. We gave photographs to the media. They took the photographs away, and nobody ran any reports on this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And because of the fighting, were there any civilian casualties at Grbavica and did you get any information about Lukavica, Hadzici, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, did you get any information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. We'd receive reports almost daily. There were casualties in Grbavica, lots of casualties, in Ilidza, Nedzarici, Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you try through the media, the TV channels or the reporters that came to see you to disseminate any of the information that pertained to the civilian casualties on the side controlled by the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, we tried. We definitely tried. But was a single picture ever published in any media or anywhere. Pictures that would show how badly Grbavica had been burned down, a part of Lukavica, Nedzarici, Otis, and so on. Nothing was published at all, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you have the figures for the casualties, civilian casualties in Grbavica alone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Some 30 civilian casualties or so at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: In the period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, there must be a foundation established for the witness to give these answers. On what basis did he establish the figures of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, what's the basis for your knowledge of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the death notices that were published and through my own personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually see some of those incidents in which civilians were killed? Were you an eye-witness of any such incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Bjelica was killed in Grbavica, in Radnicka Street in front of my car. Majstorovic Zelko was killed at Dervisa Novica Street above a staircase. Those two girls that were killed at Grbavica. Bosko Radan at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. It's not necessary. You've told us enough. Could you please tell us whether you saw what happened with the houses and the apartments that were there in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, any apartments in the first row of houses facing the Miljacka and the separation line, nobody could live there, and it was impossible to get in there, inside those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-5358.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 4358.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what building is this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The sky-scraper next to the Miljacka. Opposite Bristol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far was this from your workplace at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It's 100 metres away from my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges where the damage comes from. Were you an eye-witness of the events that caused this and can you tell us what caused the damage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I only saw the building on fire. It was set alight by explosives. I'm not a specialist in heavy weapons and such-like things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was hit by heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties in these flats as a result of these activities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Of course there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this photograph be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly, the -- I'd like to inquire as to the time-period. 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, when did this take place and I'm -- well, okay. I'll proceed in cross on those other issues. But at least to have a time-period, I would be grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the time-period? Witness, what time are you speaking of here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you another building, and let me ask you this: Was this the case with most of the buildings at Grbavica? I will not mention all the places, but let me show you DD00-4232, which is another building. I will complete my examination quite soon. What building is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This is the Unioninvest building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were other buildings at Grbavica like in 1994 and 1995 through to the end? Were there any activities at the time which caused damage to these buildings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were more buildings, such as this one, that were damaged by heavy weaponry, which was active both in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this photograph be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the date of this bombing? Witness, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to this particular building or to all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one was set on fire in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, counsel has not -- has not actually asked the witness on what basis he knows that this building was set alight, was he there. There has been no foundational questions for this photograph, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, why don't you ask these questions? Because it is true that we take in hearsay evidence, but the reliability of the evidence is strengthened if you lay a foundation for the witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, Witness, throughout the time-period from 1992 through 1993, 1994 to 1995, were you an eye-witness to the burning of this particular building and other buildings? Did you yourself see these events as they unfolded at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I was born near Grbavica. I grew up there. Even when I worked at Pale, I would come to Grbavica every day, because I had relatives there. I had friends and colleagues there, work associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All those years you saw this building on fire as well as hundreds of other buildings burning in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.
