utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that many people were killed in activities such as this one on the part of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's a leading question, isn't it? And you know that many people were killed. You have to do better than that, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, of course we have seen pictures of these destroyed buildings, but I would like to know if you would be able to tell us who burnt those buildings, who set these buildings on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who would be able to set fire to their own home, flat, or house. It's very difficult to talk about these things. It's inconceivable. There were mostly Serbs living there, although there were quite a few Muslims and Croats as well. I really don't see how else it could have been but for the BH army -- but the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When these buildings were destroyed, was there an exchange of fire or was it during a cease-fire; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened mostly during an exchange of fire, although quite a few occasions it would also happen during cease-fires. I would often hear conversations between soldiers of Republika Srpska and officers about the enemy side not adhering to the truce and that this compelled them to return fire. I also know that at some point in time the VRS army was strictly prohibited from firing because they lacked weapons and ammunition, as a result of the supply lines with Serbia having been severed, the supply lines of ammunition, food, and all the other necessities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness saw these events personally, can this photograph be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, actually, I don't object to the admission. But, in my submission, it is not correct that the witness has given evidence that he saw this building set alight when it was initially set alight -- in fact, the question by counsel was first -- the witness, throughout the time-period 1992 through to 1993, 1994, 1995, were you an eye-witness to the burning of this particular building and other buildings. Do you -- did you yourself see these events as they unfolded at the time. And the answer was: I was born near Grbavica, I grew up there. Even when I worked at Pale, I would come to Grbavica every day because I had relatives there. I had friends and colleagues there, work associates. In my submission, there is no direct answer to the question which contained two or three components as to whether he saw this building set alight initially. As I said, I don't object to the admission but I can't see how this witness can add anything to this photograph, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Witness, did you actually see this building set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course -- well, I saw the building as it was on fire, because it was burning for two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, in any event, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D348, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the building called Soping?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I know that Biljana Plavsic lived in that building. It's a sky-scraper that was targeted from all sorts of weapons. There were only civilians there, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does the word "Soping" mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, it was a small shopping mall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the civilians who would go to this Soping building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Half of the civilians were moved out because there had been victims among them and were found accommodation elsewhere. They moved to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, a moment ago you said that some sites were marked as a dangerous because of sniper fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a photograph, DD00-4269. What does this round say, this circle say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Beware of snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many such sign posts did you see at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: At least 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can DD00-4269 be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can be allowed to show another photograph to the witness and put some questions to him concerning the photographs and some other matters. He mentioned those protective screens. Perhaps he can explain what can be seen on the photograph I have here, which is DD00-4270.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what building this is? Is this what you were referring to a moment ago when you mentioned protective screens, screens that were to protect passers-by?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, this building is located at the upper end of Lenjenska Street. Some of my work associates had flats there, and I would go there to help them move out. First we had these fences, as you can see, these walls and later on we would put up blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to move in the same way this person we can see in the photograph is moving?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: But of course. All of us had to walk around Grbavica this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what is this fence facing? What -- from which direction does it protect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: From the Wilson Promenade to the Bosnian government building, the faculty of philosophy, the Museum of the Revolution, this is what this fence is facing. It's facing the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you explain to the Judges in what time-period between 1992 and 1995, or rather the 21st of November of 1995, in what time-period did the buildings at Grbavica suffer the most damage as we saw it here and on other photographs, in what period?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I asked you something else. In 1992, that doesn't mean anything. What happened in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995 there was a cease-fire. I think it was supposed to be in force until May, but the BH army forces launched a fierce attack against us. I think it was at the Djukica Potok and Zlatiste and Grbavica, the whole of Grbavica. Quite a lot of the Republika Srpska army troops were killed and I think that the line in the direction of Trebevic, Mount Trebevic was actually penetrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about military issues. I'm asking you about civilians and buildings in Sarajevo -- no, not in Sarajevo -- or, rather, yes, in Sarajevo, in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand your question. What do you mean what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the fierce attack you started talking about the military impact of the attack. But I want to ask you this combat that took place after May, what impact did it have on the civilian life, the civilian buildings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I know that the faculty of forestry was shelled. I also know that a large building called Mis was also shelled. The people started moving out of Grbavica along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, but I would like to ask this photograph that's on our screens now to be admitted into evidence. That's DD00-4270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D350, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. And Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good -- it's just -- good afternoon, Mr. Bjelica. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution and I shall ask you a couple of questions, actually more than a couple of questions today. Firstly, can I just -- may I just confirm with you that you were the editor of the Sarajevske Srpkse Novine from 1992 through to 1995, in other words during the whole period of the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: From the 13th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right, right, that's correct. And then up until 1993, you worked at the Republika Srpska government in Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the newspaper that you edited, was it -- was it a civilian -- was it -- yes, a civilian publication, if I put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you gave evidence that it was distributed throughout the military, at least in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. The military could not distribute the paper. We distributed the -- the civilians distributed it, but just a couple of copies would reach the troops at the front line, at the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I don't believe my question was that the military distributed. But you agree that the military would receive copies of your newspaper?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you gave evidence also that you -- you stated that the international media applied different standards when they were covering the area controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the area controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. You remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And of course to -- to establish that or to make that determination, you would have to be monitoring the international media on a regular basis; is that right? When you could.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, when I could, that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it, then, you're referring to the reports from these international media companies, as you said CNN and other major companies, you're referring to the reports of the shelling and sniping of the civilians within the city of Sarajevo, in other words, within the area controlled by the ABiH. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish, sir on what basis you are speaking about the differing standards and what I'm suggesting to you is that the international media would -- would compile reports or stories about the shelling and sniping or the suffering of civilians inside the city of Sarajevo more than the -- the suffering of Serb civilians in -- in the Serbian part of Sarajevo. Is that -- is that what you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. And through the Bosnia-Herzegovina TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you were also monitoring the TV from Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, may I ask you, sir, that at any time during the conflict were you a soldier with the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No, not a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it you never carried a weapon, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I never carried a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in terms of the specific military operations or the -- the exact locations of the confrontation lines and SRK positions, you really don't have complete knowledge of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I do have knowledge about the separation lines because I went there to interview soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how often would you go to the confrontation lines to interview soldiers and officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I went from one battalion and then to another battalion, and I would spend ten to 15 days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are you speaking about the battalions within the 1st Sarajevo Brigade? In other words, south of the Miljacka in Grbavica, Vraca, Trebevic? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. Vogosca, Ilidza, that's where I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you visited all these positions from 1993 through to 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that visiting the confrontation lines would have been a dangerous endeavour, considering there was a war going on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I have to tell you that it -- I had to drive 150 -- 130 to 150 kilometres to get from Grbavica to Ilidza. It was an arduous road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And yet, sir, you gave evidence that you never once took the Lukavica-Pale road, in other words the Zlatiste road, is that right, or did you in fact travel on that road, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Please, when I went from Grbavica, Lukavica, Tilava, Trebevic and then below Mount Jahorina, I don't remember what this place was called, and then I would get to Pale. And from Pale through Nahorevo, I visited all the lines and by the time I got to Vogosca, I had to take a detour to get back to Ilidza. I didn't take the Zlatiste-Trebevic road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You never took that road throughout the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I have to tell you one thing. During the cease-fire in 1994 - I don't know when it was - a bus with school children headed from Zlatiste to Trebevic and five or six children were wounded by a shell that was fired by the BH army, and I did pass through this road a couple of times during the cease-fire. That's what I said. So I didn't say that I never ever took this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps your earlier answer was not recorded properly but I have it that you never took that road. But, okay, I understand you now, that you did indeed take that road. Incidentally, when you said that the bus was hit, how did you know that the bus was hit by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Because it was fired from Colina Kapa and my son was on this bus. He went on a school trip with his class. He was in the 8th grade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it that because the ABiH had positions at Colina Kapa it's only -- it's a logical conclusion that the fire came from that position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, as you spent much time in Grbavica and you've given evidence about particular buildings that -- that were hit, you also mentioned that some of them or one of them was hit during an exchange of fire. So I take it that on occasions the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps would also fire into the city. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No, no, never from the Grbavica area. Yes, with infantry weapons, but never with heavy weapons because there weren't any there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So they did fire from Grbavica with infantry weapons into the city; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Since you have told the Court that you visited the front lines in Grbavica, do you know where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps fired from in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you not visit Sarajevo-Romanija Corps positions in Grbavica when you interviewed the soldiers, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I visited them, the front lines. That's what I said. I said that I visited the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So where did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers fire -- where in Grbavica did they fire from into the city? So you've given evidence about fire coming from the ABiH on territory that you yourself were not present, and now I'm asking you about fire from Grbavica where you visited regularly, where you interviewed soldiers, where you went to the front lines, and you are telling the Court that you don't know from which positions the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps fired from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The exchange of fire, infantry fire, was from the positions where the wall is. That's where the trenches were, along the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, the buildings that we saw earlier in court and indeed the Soping building that you gave evidence about, isn't it -- isn't it correct, sir, that in those buildings there were Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers positioned there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I think that there were no troops there because it's a civilian building which is quite far from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Soping building, sir, in the period 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said earlier that civilians had been moved out from that building. You remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I said that the civilians had moved out, and the Soping building, it's not just one building. It's a whole complex but this building that we were talking about it's the high-rise building, a sky-scraper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed. And the complex buildings when the civilians moved out and when you went there, you must have seen Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers in those buildings, sir, I put it to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Well, there could have been no soldiers there because it was far from the front line. What would the soldiers be doing in that building? I don't understand. I -- I said what I -- what I saw. What would the soldiers be doing in that building because it was so far from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When did you go to the building, sir? Do you remember the year or the date, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, every five or six days I would go there and -- but I didn't enter into the building. The building was burnt down. Why would I go in there? I just passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I have one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, following on from my previous line of questioning, with respect to the photographs that we saw, is it not correct that the buildings were destroyed because the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had soldiers and weaponry in those buildings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It didn't have any weapons there. It's impossible to keep weapons at the Soping building because it was far from the front line and the Unioninvest building at Vrbanja Most -- it was the bridge there, it had already burned down so I can't see what they would be doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: And you couldn't open fire from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you were never in the military, were you, during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I never was in the military, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the war you never handled a sniper rifle or an infantry rifle, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you never fired a mortar from a mortar round, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I don't know even know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take also that you do not have any knowledge of military strategy or other military issues that ordinarily soldiers and commanders would have to concern themselves with; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. And you may leave with us as we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any questions -- any witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just have a very short procedural issue, Mr. President. We received on 20th of July, a filing by the Defence requesting the admission under Rule 92 bis of three witness statements, and we -- the Prosecution doesn't have any objection to these witness statements coming in. They don't concerns acts and conduct of the accused, and also obviously a recurring issue, they mostly concern the preindictment period. So it's an issue of relevancy but if these witnesses would come today and could testify there would hardly be any cross-examination on these issues. So we have no objection to these coming in via 92 bis without cross-examination. And we also do have no objection to the protective measures suggested for witness T-20. I take it that means that the witness statement would come in, if decided by Your Honours, under seal. The other two witnesses are T-40 and T-44. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.21 p.m.,
